The PKGBUILD defines standard sources: a few local files (`floorp.desktop`, `floorp.png`) and a remote tarball for each architecture, fetched from the project's official GitHub releases (`https://github.com/Floorp-Projects/Floorp`). The URLs are constructed using `$pkgver` and are consistent with the declared upstream. The checksums are provided and not set to `SKIP`, so the sources will be verified after download.

The top-level scope contains only variable assignments and array declarations. There is no command substitution, no execution of external commands, and no network activity outside of the declared `source` entries. The `pkgver()` function is not defined, so version computation relies solely on the static `pkgver` variable. Therefore, sourcing this PKGBUILD during `makepkg --nobuild --nodeps --noprepare` or `makepkg --printsrcinfo` will not execute any code, download untrusted payloads, or exfiltrate data.

All operations during this phase are limited to parsing metadata and downloading the declared sources, which is the intended and safe behavior for this stage. Malicious behavior, if any, would reside in later stages (e.g., `package()`) and will be audited separately.
</details>
<summary>SAFE: No dangerous code in sourcing phase</summary>
</security_assessment>

<details>
The PKGBUILD is for the `floorp-bin` package, a binary version of the Floorp browser, built from official GitHub releases. The source URLs point directly to the project's own release assets on GitHub (`https://github.com/Floorp-Projects/Floorp/releases/download/v${pkgver}/...`), which is expected and trustworthy for this type of package. The checksums for both x86_64 and aarch64 binaries are provided and match standard practice; there are no `SKIP` values, so integrity is verified.

The build process (`package()`) extracts the prebuilt binary, installs it under `/usr/lib/floorp`, creates symlinks, installs desktop and icon files, and disables auto-updates via a `policies.json` file. All operations are confined to the package directory and follow standard packaging practices. The use of `magick` (from ImageMagick) to resize icons is legitimate and not obfuscated. The launcher script and desktop file are templated safely.

No network calls, dynamic downloads, or execution of fetched code occurs during packaging. No sensitive data exfiltration or suspicious file operations are present. The disabling of auto-updates is a common policy in AUR binary packages to maintain system package manager control and is not malicious. The code is transparent and consistent with the stated purpose of distributing a customized Firefox-based browser.
</details>
<summary>
Standard binary packaging with no malicious behavior</summary>
</security_assessment>

This prevents the application from applying updates from any designated channel and is a common practice in repackaged or forked browsers to maintain control over update sources.

There is no executable code, network activity, file manipulation, or data exfiltration possible from this file. It is a static INI file with commented warnings against modification, indicating it is intended solely for internal application use. The content serves only to configure update behavior and does not introduce any supply-chain risks or malicious functionality.

This file aligns with standard packaging practices for browser forks distributed via AUR, where update mechanisms are often disabled to ensure users receive updates only through the package manager.
</details>

The file is licensed under the Mozilla Public License v2.0, a permissive open-source license, and includes no executable code, network requests, file operations, or system modifications.

The use of `pref()` to configure update settings is standard in Mozilla-based applications and serves a legitimate purpose in controlling how and from where updates are fetched. There is no obfuscation, suspicious encoding, or use of dangerous commands. The file does not exfiltrate data or introduce backdoors. This is a benign configuration file that aligns with upstream Firefox packaging practices.

While the preference influences update behavior, it does not, by itself, constitute a security risk. The update channel is set to "release", which points to Mozilla's official release infrastructure, not a third-party or untrusted source. This file is part of the normal browser configuration and does not deviate from expected packaging norms.
</details>
